newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: ANALYSTS PREDICT ANOTHER INTEREST RATE CUT SOON
A gloomy business outlook for the next three months has convinced some analysts there will be another official interest rate cut in August.
Profits are expected to be down, medium and large businesses believe jobs will be shed, and sales growth is tipped to rise by just 0.7 per cent.
These results apply across Australian industry, not just the perceived weak sectors of manufacturing and retail.
Even construction sales are seen as falling, despite evidence of a pick-up in central Sydney, especially with Olympic Games projects.
Looking a full year ahead, business expects only mild improvement in general activity and in employment.
Jobs and inflation figures are due out in coming weeks.
And Colonial State Bank Senior economist, Craig James, believes inflation will have fallen in the June quarter, providing a good lead-in to another easing in monetary policy, early next month.
GOVT HOPEFUL OF AGREEMENT AT DEATHS IN CUSTORY SUMMIT
The Federal Government remains hopeful agreement will be reached at the Black Deaths in Custody Summit in Canberra, on a new approach to keep more indigenous people out of jail.
The Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, has expressed optimism a joint communique will emerge at the end of the talks, scheduled to conclude shortly.
ATSIC Commissioner, Col Dillon, has expressed similar optimism, and has rejected Northern Territory Attorney-General Denis Bourke's claim the summit is just a talk-fest and a waste of time and money.

Summit chair, Federal Attorney-General Daryl Willaims, says such a large gathering of state and territory ministers and indigenous representatives, indicates the genuine interest they share in finding a solution to the problem.
STATION OWNER SAYS BOAT PEOPLE SHOW COAST LINE VULNERABLE
A station owner in Western Australia's north says the recovery of 15 boat people yesterday highlights the vulnerability of the State's coastline.
Carol French's station adjoins the camping ground, north of Coral Bay, where the group of men was found yesterday, 1,100 kilometres north of Perth.
Immigration officers are taking them to Port Hedland where they will be detained for questioning.
Authorities have been told the men were travelling on a Taiwanese trawler that dropped them off near the coast.
Mrs French says it appears the men paid 300,000 Ruppea each for the voyage, or almost $A7,000.
She says coastal surveillence near Coral Bay was stopped years ago, and she believes that has left the area open to illegal visitors.
Mrs French says it is not simply an issue of people coming into the country, but also a question of how easy it is to bring drugs into Australia.
FEDERAL GOVT SIGNS LEGAL AID AGREEMENT WITH TERRITORY
The Federal Government has signed an agreement with the Northern Territory to continue funding legal aid.
The agreement provides for joint funding over the next three years worth $2.03 million.
Territory Attorney-General Denis Burke says it means Territorians remain well protected and have continued access to legal aid.
He says the negotiations have resulted in no reduction to federal funding for the Territory.
Mr Burke says the Commonwealth has also agreed to conduct needs-based funding analysis over the period of the agreement.
Federal Attorney-General Daryl Williams says formal agreements on legal aid are almost complete with all states and territories.
He says it is business as usual for people receiving legal aid assistance.
MINING COMPANIES SAY GOLD SELL-OFF NAIVE
A group representing 78 mining and exploration companies says the Reserve Bank's major sell-off of gold assets will be seriously felt right across the gold industry.
The Association of Mining and Exploration Companies says the industry is already suffering from a cyclical downturn in prices.
Association Chief Executive, George Savell, says the Reserve Bank sale sends the wrong signals to investors, and has helped push down the price of gold.
Mr Savell says the Reserve Bank will rue the decision because of the damage it will cause to the industry.
Mr Savell says if the Gold industry suffers a downturn, it is not just gold companies which will be affected, but the hundreds of thousands of ordinary Australians who invest in the companies.
He says the Government has made a naive decision, and believes it should have thought through the commercial implications.
WARNING ABOUT HOUSING-INDUCED POVERTY IN SYDNEY, MELBOURNE

A warning today that the cycle of housing-induced poverty will continue in Melbourne and Sydney, unless the Federal Government provides tax breaks to stimulate investment in the private rental market.
The Real Estate Institute of Victoria has warned rents could go higher, with many people already paying an insupportable level of income to landlords.
The Real Estate Institute says the private rental sector has shrunk in both Melbourne and Sydney.
The vacancy rate is at a critically low 1.5 per cent, instead of the accepted benchmark of 3 per cent.
The shortage may be a boon for landlords who can force rents up, but in some cases people are spending 41 per cent of their income just to rent a one bedroom flat.
Norman Huon, from the Real Estate Institute, has warned the Federal Government it must provide tax breaks.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
